summary:
AquaGuard: Seeing Water Infrastructure Through Satellite Radar

Millions of cubic metres of drinking water are lost every year through aging underground pipelines, wasting valuable water, energy and resources. Detecting these hidden problems remains a major challenge for water utilities worldwide.

AquaGuard is an interactive platform that combines NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite radar observations, real water-pipeline networks, historical repair records and machine learning to support smarter infrastructure monitoring.

Our platform brings together 1,691 documented repairs, 624 kilometres of pipelines and 24 NISAR radar acquisitions from a water district in Texas. Users can explore infrastructure on an interactive map, examine satellite observations over time and compare radar imagery before and after documented repairs.

We also developed a dataset of 3,014 labelled radar samples and a gradient-boosting model that ranks pipelines by historical failure risk.

By making complex satellite data accessible and connecting it to real infrastructure, AquaGuard addresses the challenge of understanding surface changes through SAR.

Our goal is to help utilities prioritize investigations, reduce unnecessary inspections and ultimately contribute to conserving water, while recognizing that satellite anomalies require further validation before leaks can be confirmed.
details:
AquaGuard: Seeing Water Infrastructure Through Satellite Radar

Every day, enormous quantities of clean water are lost through aging underground pipelines. In Bulgaria alone, approximately 425 million cubic metres of water were physically lost during transportation in 2024. Beyond the environmental impact, these losses represent wasted energy, higher operating costs, damaged infrastructure and increasing pressure on limited water resources.

The challenge is simple: How can water utilities identify vulnerable infrastructure when most of it is buried underground?

AquaGuard is an open-source, interactive platform that combines NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite radar observations with real water-pipeline networks, historical repair records and machine learning. Our goal is to help utilities understand changes around their infrastructure and prioritize areas for further investigation.

What We Built

Our primary demonstration focuses on the Coryell City Water Supply District in Texas, using real utility records and satellite observations.

The platform allows users to explore:

  • 1,691 documented water-pipeline repairs displayed on an interactive map.
  • 624 kilometres of pipeline infrastructure, including pipe characteristics and pressure zones.
  • 24 NISAR satellite acquisitions, allowing users to investigate how the surrounding landscape changes over time.
  • Before-and-after radar comparisons around documented repair locations.
  • Machine-learning risk rankings highlighting pipeline sections with higher historical failure risk.

We also developed a dataset containing 3,014 NISAR radar samples, including 274 documented repair locations and 2,740 comparison samples. This provides a foundation for training and evaluating future satellite-based leak-screening models.

How It Works

AquaGuard connects three sources of information: infrastructure records, satellite observations and historical failure patterns.

First, we collect pipeline locations and documented repairs from publicly accessible utility records. We then match those locations with NISAR radar acquisitions and process the satellite imagery into comparable observations.

Our interactive platform lets users select a pipeline repair, move through the satellite timeline and examine radar imagery from before and after the event.

In parallel, a gradient-boosting machine-learning model analyzes historical repairs and pipeline characteristics to rank infrastructure by break risk.

The result is an accessible decision-support tool that turns complex infrastructure and satellite datasets into information that utilities can explore and investigate.

What Makes AquaGuard Different?

Rather than presenting satellite imagery as an isolated scientific product, AquaGuard connects it directly to real-world infrastructure, documented failures and operational decisions.

Our approach combines an interactive radar explorer, historical risk modelling and a reusable labelled satellite dataset within one open-source project.

We also prioritize scientific transparency. Our experiments have not yet demonstrated a reliable standalone satellite signature of individual pipeline leaks, nor a proven improvement in break-risk prediction from adding NISAR observations. The platform therefore presents radar changes as investigation evidence, not confirmed leak detections.

Technologies Used

We developed AquaGuard using Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, MapLibre GL JS and machine learning with gradient-boosted decision trees.

Our data-processing workflow uses NumPy, Pandas, GeoPandas, Rasterio, HDF5 processing tools and NASA Earthdata services. The primary satellite data comes from NASA-ISRO NISAR, supported by publicly accessible utility GIS datasets and geographic reference layers.

Intended Impact

AquaGuard aims to support smarter water-infrastructure management by helping utilities prioritize inspections, better understand environmental changes near pipelines and make more informed maintenance decisions.

If validated and deployed operationally, this approach could help reduce unnecessary inspections, accelerate the investigation of suspected failures, conserve drinking water, reduce wasted pumping energy and improve infrastructure resilience.

Our vision is to transform satellite observations into practical evidence for protecting one of our most essential resources: water.
